newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ markets relaxed despite knife-edge election.
newsitem.headline: NZ markets relaxed despite knife-edge election.

text.p: A change of New Zealand government could stall an easing in monetary conditions, but financial markets seem unfazed by the prospect, economists say.
Warnings by Prime Minister Jim Bolger that a left-wing coalition would wreak economic turmoil have failed to spook markets in the run-up to a general election on October 12.

"The extent to which bond yields have come off in the past few days has to cast doubt on whether there's much political risk priced in at all at the moment, which is somewhat of a concern given that the polls are pointing to a fairly finely balanced election", said David Drage, economist at ANZ Bank.

Opinion polls suggest the three main opposition parties -- Labour, economic nationalist New Zealand First and the left-wing Alliance -- may win enough seats between them to topple the conservative National Party government.

Despite the uncertainty, 10-year bond yields have fallen to 7.85 percent from 8.49 percent in the past month, 90-day bank bill rates have eased to 9.85 percent from 9.97 percent, and the currency remains around 70 U.S. cents, near eight-year highs.

While this strength could limit the extent of any post-election rally, economists expect interest rates to fall under a right-of-centre government, and the currency to remain around its present level.
"When and how monetary policy is brought from tight to neutral will depend on the election outcome," said Bancorp executive director Roger Kerr.

"If it's a right-of-centre National victory, a continuation of current policies, we think that adjustment in monetary policy will come through lower short-term interest rates and not so much in the currency.
"In other words, we'll get quite a sharp fall in short-term interest rates through October, November, December..."
However, if a Labour-led, left-of-centre coalition government were to emerge from the election, the general expectation was for higher rates and a lower currency.
"Certainly people would sell the short end of the (yield) curve," said an economist who declined to be named.
Labour's intention to widen the Reserve Bank's target band for underlying inflation to minus one to three percent from 0-2 percent would not allow an easing in monetary conditions.
"There would be a slightly more easy fiscal policy, which means monetary policy won't be able to change its stance at all," the economist said.
But the markets were showing little fear of such a result, partly reflecting confidence in Labour finance spokesman Michael Cullen as a prospective finance minister.

Bolger's warnings that a left-wing government would undo 10 years of reform set him at odds with ratings agency Standard and Poor, which said it did not regard the election as a threat to New Zealand's AA+ foreign currency credit rating.

"It's a common enough occurrence around the world that election uncertainty is taken most bearishly by local participants, people who can't see the forest for the trees," said Bank of New Zealand economist Peter Jolly.

"Some of the changes that are mooted by opposition parties won't be treated that favourably by markets, so you'll get things repriced, but there is a limit to the downside, whereas some people in New Zealand think there isn't."
